title: Crisafulli to defy PM, pitch alternative plan for data centres
full_text:
David Crisafulli will pitch Anthony Albanese and state leaders an alternative framework for approving power-hungry data centres, requiring mandatory local consultation, protection of water supply, and no renewable energy directive.
The Queensland Premier is preparing for a fight at this week’s national cabinet meeting on AI, where his state and the Northern Territory are the only holdouts to the federal government’s decree for the $150bn data centre industry to be fuelled entirely by renewable power.
Energy Minister Chris Bowen on Sunday said the Albanese government would consider using constitutional powers to override Queensland’s objections to the proposed federal rules.
“We’re not going to let Queensland run a race to the bottom, which would see energy bills go up, reliability go down, because they want data centres at any cost,” Mr Bowen said.
“With the right rules in place, you can actually get the investment, but actually get to a good outcome where those data centres need to bring their own renewable energy and can back it up with gas peaking. That’s sensible. The Queensland government’s approach is not sensible. We won’t let them set the rules for the whole country.”
Mr Crisafulli’s Liberal National Party government is developing a planning framework for approving data centres that will mirror legislation passed last year for major solar and wind farms and battery energy storage facilities.
Under the Queensland reforms, the state government will be responsible for co-ordinating and assessing any data centre applications, taking the power away from Queensland’s 77 local councils and ensuring a consistent approach across the state.
But proponents must negotiate social impact assessments and community benefit agreements with the relevant local government before a state development application can be lodged.
Data centre developers would also have to prove their operations would not threaten agricultural or residential water supply, but would be able to nominate their own “market-driven energy mix” that could include fossil fuels or renewables.
Under Queensland’s plan, proposed data centres would be assessed in the same way as mining, renewable energy or agricultural projects.
Mr Crisafulli told The Australian the planning framework was designed to show the burgeoning industry the state was “open for business and a place to invest again”, while listening to community voices.
“This is about data sovereignty for our country, it’s about respecting communities’ wishes and resources, and it’s about creating the jobs of tomorrow while protecting the Queensland of today,” he said.
Deputy Premier Jarrod Bleijie said Queensland was driven by outcomes while Canberra was “driven by ideology”.
“We disagree with Canberra that only renewables must be used when we have an abundance of coal, gas and renewables in Queensland,” Mr Bleijie said.
Queensland and the NT, at an energy ministers meeting in July, officially opposed the commonwealth’s commitment to legislate national minimum standards requiring large-scale data centres to underwrite renewable power supply.
The Minns NSW Labor government this month released its data centre policy framework, requiring data centre investment to be matched with increased investment in renewable energy and water infrastructure to access streamlined approvals.
If operators were able to meet the state’s new guidelines – including imposing no net cost to consumers and communities, and funding additional supply of water and energy – their plans will be assessed within 75 days.
Regulations will also be changed to make sure data centres pay for any required upgrades to the energy network.
At the time, NSW Energy Minister Penny Sharpe said that as demand for data centre increased, NSW needed to ensure the necessary infrastructure was there to support the sector.
“These reforms will make sure data centre growth drives investment in renewable energy, while holding operators to the highest air quality standards,” Ms Sharpe said.
There are already 19 data centres in NSW, worth about $50bn, and another 60 are under construction.
